opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think compute scarcity is honestly one of the most underrated forces shaping how the field actually moves. The clearest example people point to is DeepSeek. When you're working under export controls and you can't just buy another hundred thousand H100s, you're forced to get really creative at every layer of the stack. That's where you see things like their mixture-of-experts designs with very fine-grained experts, multi-head latent attention to shrink the KV cache, FP8 training, and even going down below CUDA to hand-tune communication between GPUs. Those aren't flashy research ideas on their own, but together they add up to a huge efficiency gain, and they came out of necessity.

The interesting contrast is with the big American labs. They're not compute-unconstrained either, which people sometimes miss. Everyone at OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google will tell you they're compute-limited, but the constraint shows up differently. It's less "we can't train this model at all" and more "we have to choose between training the next frontier run, serving hundreds of millions of users, and giving researchers enough GPUs to run experiments." So efficiency pressure shows up in inference costs and in how you allocate internally, and a lot of the cleverness goes into serving rather than pretraining.

I'd also say scarcity changes research culture. When compute is abundant, the easiest move is to scale up and see what happens, and that's often the right move. When it's scarce, you have to run small careful experiments, trust your scaling laws, and really understand why something works before you commit a big run. That discipline tends to produce ideas that transfer. So scarcity doesn't just make labs cheaper. It changes what kind of progress they make, and sometimes it pushes the whole field forward because the tricks get published and everyone adopts them.

The caveat is that efficiency doesn't replace compute. It multiplies it. If you make training ten times more efficient, the labs with the most GPUs just use that to train an even bigger or better model. That's the Jevons paradox argument. So I don't think efficiency gains end the compute race. They reset the frontier and make the scarce players more competitive for a while.

r001.rationale: The response says DeepSeek faced compute constraints and used multi-head latent attention to shrink the KV cache, linking scarcity to a model design that improves inference efficiency.

r002.rationale: The response says American labs direct much of their efficiency work toward serving, but does not say they consider DeepSeek-style memory optimization gains too small to justify the effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that compute scarcity is probably the single biggest forcing function on how labs actually behave day to day, and it's less about the frontier than people assume.

If you're at one of the three or four labs that can run a hundred-thousand-GPU training run, scarcity shows up as prioritization. You have one or two big runs a year, and every ablation you want to do competes with that run for chips. So you get really disciplined about scaling laws and small-scale proxies. You run a thousand tiny experiments at one-hundredth or one-thousandth the scale and you bet that the trends hold. A lot of the "secret sauce" at those places is just institutional knowledge about which small-scale signals actually predict big-scale outcomes and which ones lie to you.

For everybody else, and I'd include most of open-source and a lot of academia and even well-funded startups, scarcity pushes you toward post-training and data. You can't out-pretrain OpenAI or Google. But you can take a strong open base model and do really careful instruction tuning, preference tuning, RL on verifiable tasks, and get a lot of capability for a tiny fraction of the compute. That's basically the whole story of the last couple years in open models. DeepSeek is the extreme case, where being somewhat compute-constrained pushed them into architectural choices, MoE, multi-head latent attention, FP8 training, that the big labs had less urgency to adopt because they could just buy more chips.

The thing I'd caution against is the narrative that scarcity makes everyone efficient. It doesn't. The labs with the most compute are often the least efficient per FLOP because they don't need to be, and their incentive is to convert money into capability as fast as possible, not to be elegant. Efficiency gets discovered at the edges and then gets absorbed by the center. That's a pretty healthy dynamic actually, as long as the open ecosystem keeps enough compute to stay relevant. The thing I actually worry about is the point where the gap gets so wide that the edge can't produce ideas the center cares about anymore.

r001.rationale: The response says compute constraints pushed DeepSeek toward architectural choices, but it does not say Chinese labs trained models to use less compute during inference.

r002.rationale: It says big labs had less urgency to adopt DeepSeek-associated techniques because they could buy more chips, but does not state that American labs considered memory-optimization gains too small to justify the effort.

astra-6.text:
I think scarcity forces you to be much more deliberate about where you spend compute. If you can’t get another cluster, you have to ask: Is our data good enough? Are we running the right experiments? Can we learn the same thing from a smaller run before committing to a big one? Efficiency is as much about avoiding wasted experiments as it is about making each training step faster.

And the constraint matters. A team with limited training compute might build on an existing open model and focus on post-training. A team serving a popular product might prioritize inference efficiency, because every reduction in the cost of generating a response adds up across users.

But I wouldn’t say scarcity automatically produces better research. You need enough compute to test ideas and get reliable feedback. Below that threshold, you’re just constrained. The interesting dynamic is that when labs do find an efficiency improvement, they often spend the savings on bigger models or more experiments. So efficiency can increase what they accomplish without reducing their total demand for compute.

sol-6.1.text:
Compute scarcity makes efficiency very concrete. If you have a fixed number of GPUs, getting more out of each training run can be the difference between testing an idea and never getting to it. So labs invest in better data, better training infrastructure, and experiments that tell them quickly whether something is worth scaling.

But efficiency doesn’t necessarily mean using less compute overall. Often, if you make training twice as efficient, you use that gain to train a bigger model or run more experiments. The goal is usually to get more capability out of the compute you can access.

And scarcity shapes which questions you ask. A smaller lab might pursue methods that a larger lab wouldn’t prioritize because the larger lab can afford to scale a more established approach. That can produce useful innovation, although you still need enough compute to demonstrate that your efficient method actually works at a meaningful scale.
